reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

I found 9 findings in PR 1237 (`claude-code: add timeouts to Entire hooks`). I checked them against the source but did not run anything. The most serious is a parsing regression: `entire enable` can now silently delete a user's hook matchers in some malformed configs.

    "file": "cmd/entire/cli/agent/claudecode/types.go",
    "line": 41,
    "summary": "ClaudeHookMatcher.UnmarshalJSON (and ClaudeHookEntry's on a non-type error) now returns an error that stops encoding/json decoding the array partway. parseHookType ignores parse errors and marshalHookType writes back the shortened slice, so every matcher after the bad one is deleted.",
    "failure_scenario": "Say PreToolUse in .claude/settings.json is [{matcher:5,hooks:[...]}, {matcher:\"Bash\",hooks:[user hook]}], or a matcher whose hooks array holds a bare string. Before this PR, encoding/json recorded the type error and kept decoding every element. Now the custom Unmarshaler's error is fatal: the decode stops at element 0 and leaves len=1. installHookEntries then marshals only that partial element back, and `entire enable` deletes the user's Bash matcher and its hooks."
  },

    "file": "cmd/entire/cli/doctor.go",
    "line": 1366,
    "summary": "CheckHookConfig now reports HooksOutdated when a hook only lacks its timeout. `entire status` and the doctor drift check then tell the user to run `entire enable --force`, which strips every Entire hook and rebuilds it from scratch. That throws away the timeouts and extra fields this PR is careful to keep.",
    "failure_scenario": "A user set timeout 300 on the Stop hook and added a statusMessage on the UserPromptSubmit hook, but the pre-task hook has no timeout. `entire status` shows 'claude-code hooks out of date · run entire enable --force'. Following that advice removes all Entire entries and re-adds them with the defaults, so the custom timeout and statusMessage are lost. A plain `entire enable` or `entire doctor` would only have filled in the missing timeout."

    "file": "cmd/entire/cli/agent/claudecode/hooks.go",

Claude Code cancels it at 10s and no session state is written. The later Stop or UserPromptSubmit hooks then run without a SessionStart record, which can break caller resolution and checkpoint attribution."

Doctor then prints 'OUT OF DATE, run enable --force' for a config it is about to fix itself, and the --force advice wipes user hook fields (see the previous finding). The comment misdescribes how the code behaves."

I re-reviewed PR #1237 and found 9 issues. I checked them against the source but didn't run anything.

**Fix before merge**
1. **A malformed matcher can delete the hooks after it** (`claudecode/types.go:41`). The new `UnmarshalJSON` on `ClaudeHookMatcher`/`ClaudeHookEntry` returns an error, and that stops decoding the array at the bad element. `parseHookType` ignores the error and `marshalHookType` writes back the shorter slice. Example: `PreToolUse: [{matcher:5,...}, {matcher:"Bash", hooks:[user hook]}]`. After `entire enable`, the user's Bash matcher is gone. Before this PR, the decoder recorded the error and kept going.
2. **The status advice now loses user settings** (`doctor.go:1366`). A hook that is only missing its timeout now counts as `HooksOutdated`. `entire status` then says to run `entire enable --force`, which strips every Entire hook and rebuilds it. That wipes custom timeouts and extra fields like `statusMessage`, which this PR works to keep. A plain `entire enable` or `entire doctor` would only fill in the missing timeout.

**Worth reconsidering**
3. **The SessionStart timeout may be too short** (`hooks.go:203`). 10s has to cover CLI startup, git resolution and state writes, not just the 1s network refresh. A cold start, such as the first launch after an upgrade, could go over 10s and the session's start record would never be written.
4. **A comment relies on an unverified default** (`hooks.go:205`). It says Claude Code's default timeout is 30s, but the `gitrepo/status.go` comment this PR replaces said about 60s. If the real default is longer, this quietly shortens UserPromptSubmit's budget, leaving 10s after the 20s `StatusWalkBudget`.
5. **Stale state when decoding into an existing value** (`types.go:68`). `UnmarshalJSON` doesn't reset `raw`/`extra`, so decoding again into an existing value can marshal the old bytes.

**Cleanup**
6. **Outdated comment in doctor.go** (`doctor.go:192`). It says `checkHookDrift` "does not look at timeouts", but it now does, through `HasStaleManagedHooks`.
7. **Second false comment** (`doctor.go:1377`). `checkRetiredDenyRule` still calls itself "the one doctor check that repairs without asking". `checkHookTimeouts` does that too now.
8. **Duplicated settings code** (`hooks.go:284`). `RepairHookTimeouts` repeats the read/parse/write sequence instead of reusing `loadRawClaudeSettingsForInstall`/`writeClaudeSettingsFile`, so the two code paths can drift apart.
9. **Settings file read twice** (`hooks.go:743`). `CheckHookConfig` parses `settings.json` and then `HasStaleManagedHooks` reads and parses it again. That doubles the I/O for every status and doctor call.

**Proposed review lesson** (for `General.md`):
> Do not return an error from a custom `UnmarshalJSON` on an array element for a type mismatch you could recover from; `encoding/json` stops decoding the whole array, so a later write-back drops the remaining elements. Keep the raw bytes and return nil instead.

Findings 4, 6 and 7 are the kind of mistake your existing "write comments carefully" memory already covers, so they don't need a new lesson.

Should I propose fixes for 1 and 2 (and the rest), or do you want to add the lesson first?

    32	type ClaudeHookMatcher struct {
    33		Matcher string            `json:"matcher"`
    34		Hooks   []ClaudeHookEntry `json:"hooks"`
    35		extra   map[string]json.RawMessage
    36	}
    37

    41	func (m *ClaudeHookMatcher) UnmarshalJSON(data []byte) error {
    42		extra, err := unmarshalKeepingExtra(data, (*claudeHookMatcherFields)(m), "matcher", "hooks")
    43		m.extra = extra

    46

    49	}

    51	// ClaudeHookEntry represents a single hook command
    52	type ClaudeHookEntry struct {

    54		Command string `json:"command,omitempty"`
    55		// Timeout is the hook's timeout in seconds. Omitted (0) leaves Claude Code's
    56		// default in place; set only where a hook needs an explicit budget.
    57		Timeout int `json:"timeout,omitempty"`
    58		extra   map[string]json.RawMessage
    59		// raw holds the entry as the user wrote it when a modeled field has a type

    62		raw json.RawMessage

    72			// hook; only the write-back has to use the original bytes.

entries.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

input.prompt: What is the default timeout for command hooks? Are there per-event defaults (e.g. UserPromptSubmit, SessionStart, SessionEnd)? Quote the exact sentences about timeout defaults.

toolu_014KMLXbdC85FkLuSisKX6sw.prompt: What is the default timeout for command hooks? Are there per-event defaults (e.g. UserPromptSubmit, SessionStart, SessionEnd)? Quote the exact sentences about timeout defaults.

content.content:
**Default timeout for command hooks: 600 seconds.** The reference gives this in the `timeout` row of the common fields table:

> `timeout` | no | Seconds before canceling. Claude Code doesn't enforce it on a command hook you run with [`async: true`](#run-hooks-in-the-background). Defaults: 600 for `command`, `http`, and `mcp_tool`; 30 for `prompt`; 60 for `agent`. Claude Code lowers the `command`, `http`, and `mcp_tool` default to 30 on [`UserPromptSubmit`](#userpromptsubmit), [`PreModelSwitch`](#premodelswitch), and [`PostModelSwitch`](#postmodelswitch), and to 10 on [`MessageDisplay`](#messagedisplay). [`SessionEnd`](#sessionend) hooks share a 1.5-second budget; if your settings set a longer per-hook `timeout`, Claude Code raises the budget to match, up to 60 seconds

**Per-event defaults for command hooks:**

| Event | Default timeout |
| :- | :- |
| `UserPromptSubmit` | 30 seconds |
| `PreModelSwitch` | 30 seconds |
| `PostModelSwitch` | 30 seconds |
| `MessageDisplay` | 10 seconds |
| `SessionEnd` | Shared 1.5-second budget, raised to match a longer per-hook `timeout` up to 60 seconds |

content.text:
I've checked all 9 findings against the code and Claude Code's hook docs. Two are wrong, one I'd skip, and the other six need edits. Per your working agreement, here's the plan first; I haven't edited anything yet.

**Dropping these two**
- **#1 (matchers deleted):** this doesn't happen. I ran the real `installHookEntries` on a malformed matcher (`matcher: 5`), a bare-string hook and a fractional timeout, using Go 1.27.1 (the version `go.mod` pins). Every matcher after the bad one came through intact; Go keeps decoding the rest of the array.
- **#4 (30s default unverified):** the comment is correct. Claude Code's hooks docs say command hooks default to 600s, lowered to 30s on `UserPromptSubmit`. The old "about 60s" comment was the stale one.

**Proposed fixes**
- **#2 (status sends users to `--force`):** change the `entire status` hint from `run 'entire enable --force'` to `run 'entire doctor'` (`status.go:252`).
  - Doctor already adds missing timeouts before its drift check, and it prints the `--force` advice itself for anything it can't fix.
  - So a config that's only missing timeouts gets fixed without wiping the user's own timeouts or extra fields.
  - Tradeoff: this one-line hint changes for every agent, not just Claude Code.
  - Alternative: stop counting missing timeouts as "outdated". That would undo what the previous review asked for, and status would go quiet about hooks that can still block Claude, so I don't recommend it.
- **#3 (SessionStart 10s):** raise it to 30s with its own constant.
  - Session start does more than the 1s network refresh: it stores the session hint, counts other active sessions and claims the startup message.
  - Claude Code's default for SessionStart is 600s, so 30s still bounds it tightly.
  - Tradeoff: a stalled launch would block Claude's startup for up to 30s instead of 10s.
- **#5 (stale bytes on re-decode):** reset `raw` and `extra` at the start of `ClaudeHookEntry.UnmarshalJSON`, and keep `extra` on the type-error path too.
- **#6 and #7 (wrong comments):** fix the ordering comment in `doctor.go:192` and the "one doctor check" claim in `doctor.go:1377`.
- **#8 (duplicate settings code):** rebuild `RepairHookTimeouts` on `loadRawClaudeSettingsForInstall` and `writeClaudeSettingsFile`.
  - One small behavior change: like install, the repair would then remove an empty `"permissions": {}` block. I'd update its doc comment to say so.

**Skipping**
- **#9 (settings file read twice):** it's a second read of a small JSON file during `status` and `doctor`. Fixing it means more code than the time it saves, so I'd leave it unless you want it.

**Testing:** I'd add regression tests for #2 (the hint text) and #5 (re-decoding into the same value). Then `mise run check`. Per your preference, I'll show you the commit split and messages before committing.

Should I go ahead with this plan, the `entire doctor` hint for #2 and 30s for SessionStart?

# General Review Lessons

- Make a guard's zero-match check count only the matches it is meant to protect. Matches that are always present, like the guard's own allowed cases, keep the check from ever firing.
- Test a guard by planting a violation and by breaking its detection, and see it fail both times. A guard that passes on clean code proves nothing.

- Before setting an explicit timeout, look up the platform's current default for that exact event; an explicit value can shorten the budget rather than add one.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

I fixed six of the nine review findings. `mise run check` failed on four tests in parts of the code this change doesn't touch; all four passed when I re-ran them on their own.

**What changed**
- **#2, status advice:** `entire status` now says `run 'entire doctor'` for outdated hooks instead of `run 'entire enable --force'`. Doctor adds missing timeouts in place and still names the `--force` fix for anything it can't repair. This hint changes for every agent, as agreed.
- **#3, SessionStart timeout:** it's now 30s, in its own `sessionStartHookTimeoutSec` constant, and I updated the repo's own `.claude/settings.json` to match.
- **#5, stale bytes on re-decode:** both custom `UnmarshalJSON` methods now reset the value before decoding, so leftover bytes from an earlier decode can't be written back.
- **#6 and #7, wrong comments:** fixed both doctor comments.
- **#8, duplicate settings code:** `RepairHookTimeouts` now uses `loadRawClaudeSettingsForInstall` and `writeClaudeSettingsFile`.
  - As planned, an empty `"permissions": {}` block is now removed. I changed the existing test to use a non-empty permissions block so it still checks the block is kept.
  - One difference I didn't mention up front: a read error other than "file missing" is now treated as no config, the same as install, instead of being logged as a warning.

**Dropped:** #1 (it doesn't reproduce on Go 1.27.1) and #4 (Claude Code's hooks docs confirm the 30s default). **Skipped:** #9.

**Verification**
- Lint: 0 issues.
- New tests: `TestRunStatus_HooksOutdatedPointsToDoctor` and `TestClaudeHookEntry_RedecodeDropsKeptBytes` both failed before the fix and pass after.
- Full test run: everything else passed. The four failures were `TestProbeConfigDir_AsksClaude` and `TestResolveClaudeConfigDir_PrefersClaudesAnswer` (5s timeouts), plus `TestInstallHooks_ForeignWrapperOverPreGuardEntireDoesNotRecurse` and `TestInstallHooks_ReclaimedChainRunsEachHookOnce` (killed at 10s). They test the Claude config probe and git hook backups, and look like load timeouts.
- The diff passes every lesson in `General.md` and `cli.md`.

**Proposed commit:** one commit with these 7 files, leaving the three untracked `docs/*.html` files out. Per your commit-message preference there's no attribution trailer, so the message is just:

```
fix(claude-code): point outdated hooks to doctor, give SessionStart 30s, and reuse the settings writer for timeout repair
```

Should I commit it?

claude-code: add timeouts to Entire hooks
=====
fixes #1065

Gives each of Entire's Claude Code hooks a timeout, so Claude Code cancels a stalled `entire` launch and keeps going instead of waiting on it. Existing installs get the timeouts from `entire doctor` or their next `entire enable`, and `entire status` flags configs that still lack them.

#### why

In #1065, macOS blocks `entire` before Go `main()` runs (`_dyld_start`), so nothing inside the binary can time out. Without a hook `timeout`, Claude Code kept waiting on the stuck hook (still blocked after 40s in testing), and stuck hook processes piled up across sessions. With a `timeout` set, Claude Code cancels the hook and continues.

#### what changed

- Each Entire hook now carries its own timeout, from one shared table that install and repair both read. Claude Code's default is 600s for command hooks and 30s for `UserPromptSubmit`:
  - **10s** for `session-start`, which Claude blocks startup on. Its only network call is a trail refresh capped at 1s.
  - **30s** for `user-prompt-submit`, `subagent-start` and `pre-task`, which snapshot the worktree. This matches Claude Code's own `UserPromptSubmit` default and stays above `gitrepo.StatusWalkBudget` (20s), so a slow status walk degrades on its own before the hook is cancelled.
  - **120s** for `stop`, `stop-failure`, `subagent-stop` and `post-task`, which write checkpoint data. Their path can spend up to 15s on a remote probe (`WriteProbeFetchBudget`) and 20s on a first-checkpoint status (`StatusWalkBudget`) before transcript work, and a 65MB transcript has been seen taking 30s (#2115).
  - **None** for `session-end`. Claude Code already gives exit hooks only a short time, and an explicit timeout would make it wait longer.
- New hooks are written with their timeout. `entire enable` adds the timeout to existing Entire hooks that have none, keeps any timeout the user set, and says it updated outdated hooks instead of "already installed".
- `entire doctor` adds the missing timeouts without asking, as it already does for the retired deny rule, and does so before its hook drift check so that check reports on the repaired config. The repair only sets a timeout on an Entire hook that has none: it adds, removes and moves no hook, keeps the user's timeouts, skips a hook type that does not parse, and rewrites only the `hooks` block.
- The Claude Code drift check used by `entire status` and `entire doctor` now reports hooks as out of date whenever a plain install would rewrite them, including Entire hooks in a command shape an older CLI wrote (which the repair does not match) and hooks without their timeout.
- Rewriting `settings.json` keeps fields Entire does not model on the user's own hooks and matchers (for example `async`, `statusMessage`, prompt hooks). Only exact-case keys are decoded, so a key like `"Command"` is kept as written instead of overwriting `command`, and an entry whose modeled field has another type (such as a fractional `timeout`) is written back unchanged.
- The repo's own `.claude/settings.json` is updated to match.

#### test plan

- [x] Install tests: each hook's timeout on a fresh install, timeouts added to an existing install, a user-set timeout kept, a second install not rewriting the file, user hook fields kept, and a fresh install not reported as outdated.
- [x] Field preservation: differently-cased keys and a fractional timeout survive an install unchanged, and a fractional timeout on an Entire hook is neither backfilled nor reported as outdated.
- [x] Repair tests: an untimed Entire hook next to a user's own matcher, a malformed hook type and `"permissions": {}` (only the timeout changes, a second run changes nothing), no settings file (nothing created), and a user-set timeout (file untouched).
- [x] Drift check: missing timeouts and an older command shape both report outdated until an install fixes them.
- [x] Doctor test: a config with its timeouts removed reports out of date, is repaired to exactly what `enable` writes, then reports OK, and a second repair prints nothing.
- [x] `mise run check` (two unrelated tests, `TestExternalCommand_SigintReachesPlugin` and `TestProbeConfigDir_AsksClaude`, each failed once under full-suite load and passed when rerun)
- [x] Manual check with the real binary in a temp repo:
  - A fresh `entire enable` reports only the installed hooks.
  - After the timeouts were removed by hand, `entire enable` and `entire doctor` each restored a file byte-for-byte identical to a fresh enable, and a second `doctor` run printed nothing.
- [x] Manual check with real Claude Code and a fake `entire` on `PATH` that hangs forever (run with the earlier 10s value for prompt hooks):
  - `session-start` was killed at 9.9s and `user-prompt-submit` at 10.1s.
  - `session-end` was cut off by Claude's exit limit at 1.5s, and Claude still answered.

#### not in scope

- Git hooks (`prepare-commit-msg`, `post-commit`, ...) can still hang `git commit` in this state.
- Pi already applies a flat 10s timeout in its generated extension. Whether that suits each Pi hook is better tracked in #2115.

In entireio/cli the quality bar is *evidence*, not code volume. Stefan Haubold (`Soph`) wrote 25 of the last 60 commits as of 2026-08-14 and sets the house style. Diffs are often tiny (#1985 was +6/-1); PR bodies are lab notebooks.

The beat order every exemplar PR follows: **Problem** (failure quoted verbatim, real log/CI output) → **Cause** (traced to a specific commit, often by diffing logs from the last green run) → **Fix** (framed as removing an asymmetry, reusing an existing helper, not adding a mechanism) → **Why nothing caught it** (explicit coverage-gap post-mortem) → **Tests, "Verified RED"** (named tests plus the exact pre-fix failure message) → **Rejected alternatives** (with cost, e.g. "~4 signatures and ~45 call sites") → **Test plan checkboxes** ending in `mise run check`.

Two habits worth copying: performance claims use **interleaved** A/B runs with medians (sequential runs let the first arm absorb cold page-cache cost and invert the result — stated in both #1985 and #1968), and negative/deflated results get reported honestly (#1985 talked itself down from a 49% headline to 2%).

**Why:** matching this format is the highest-leverage thing for getting contributions merged fast, and it is doable before deep Go fluency.
**How to apply:** write the failing test first so its real output becomes the "Verified RED" line — the test discipline and the PR-body discipline are the same act. Full playbook artifact: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0228a8ac-84b6-413e-bd05-5621d7dfb4f3 . See [[entire-1927-contribution-thread]].

fixes #1065

Gives each of Entire's Claude Code hooks a timeout, so Claude Code cancels a stalled `entire` launch and keeps going instead of waiting on it. Existing installs get the timeouts from `entire doctor` or their next `entire enable`, and `entire status` flags configs that still lack them and points to `entire doctor`.

#### why

In #1065, macOS blocks `entire` before Go `main()` runs (`_dyld_start`), so nothing inside the binary can time out. Without a hook `timeout`, Claude Code kept waiting on the stuck hook (still blocked after 40s in testing), and stuck hook processes piled up across sessions. With a `timeout` set, Claude Code cancels the hook and continues.

#### what changed

- Each Entire hook now carries its own timeout, from one shared table that install and repair both read. Claude Code's default is 600s for command hooks and 30s for `UserPromptSubmit`:
  - **30s** for `session-start`, which Claude blocks startup on. Besides a trail refresh capped at 1s, it resolves the repo and reads and writes session state, which a cold start or a large repo can slow well past that. This is still far below the 600s default.
  - **30s** for `user-prompt-submit`, `subagent-start` and `pre-task`, which snapshot the worktree. This matches Claude Code's own `UserPromptSubmit` default and stays above `gitrepo.StatusWalkBudget` (20s), so a slow status walk degrades on its own before the hook is cancelled.
  - **120s** for `stop`, `stop-failure`, `subagent-stop` and `post-task`, which write checkpoint data. Their path can spend up to 15s on a remote probe (`WriteProbeFetchBudget`) and 20s on a first-checkpoint status (`StatusWalkBudget`) before transcript work, and a 65MB transcript has been seen taking 30s (#2115).
  - **None** for `session-end`. Claude Code already gives exit hooks only a short time, and an explicit timeout would make it wait longer.
- New hooks are written with their timeout. `entire enable` adds the timeout to existing Entire hooks that have none, keeps any timeout the user set, and says it updated outdated hooks instead of "already installed".
- `entire doctor` adds the missing timeouts without asking, as it already does for the retired deny rule, and does so before its hook drift check so that check reports on the repaired config. The repair only sets a timeout on an Entire hook that has none: it adds, removes and moves no hook, keeps the user's timeouts, and skips a hook type that does not parse. It reads and writes `settings.json` through the same helpers as install, so an emptied `permissions` block is dropped the same way.
- The Claude Code drift check used by `entire status` and `entire doctor` now reports hooks as out of date whenever a plain install would rewrite them, including Entire hooks in a command shape an older CLI wrote (which the repair does not match) and hooks without their timeout. `entire status` now suggests `entire doctor` instead of `entire enable --force` for outdated hooks: doctor adds missing timeouts in place and names the fix for anything else, while `--force` rebuilds every Entire hook and drops the timeouts and fields the user set on them.
- Rewriting `settings.json` keeps fields Entire does not model on the user's own hooks and matchers (for example `async`, `statusMessage`, prompt hooks). Only exact-case keys are decoded, so a key like `"Command"` is kept as written instead of overwriting `command`, and an entry whose modeled field has another type (such as a fractional `timeout`) is written back unchanged. Decoding resets each entry first, so bytes kept from an earlier decode never replace the entry that followed.
- The repo's own `.claude/settings.json` is updated to match.

#### test plan

- [x] Install tests: each hook's timeout on a fresh install, timeouts added to an existing install, a user-set timeout kept, a second install not rewriting the file, user hook fields kept, and a fresh install not reported as outdated.
- [x] Field preservation: differently-cased keys and a fractional timeout survive an install unchanged, and a fractional timeout on an Entire hook is neither backfilled nor reported as outdated.
- [x] Repair tests: an untimed Entire hook next to a user's own matcher, a malformed hook type and a permissions block (only the timeout changes, a second run changes nothing), no settings file (nothing created), and a user-set timeout (file untouched).
- [x] Drift check: missing timeouts and an older command shape both report outdated until an install fixes them.
- [x] Status hint: `entire status` points outdated hooks to `entire doctor`, not `entire enable --force` (verified RED: the output still said `run 'entire enable --force'`).
- [x] Re-decoding: decoding a clean entry into a value that held a fractional timeout writes back the clean entry (verified RED: the old `"command":"a","timeout":1.5` came back).
- [x] Doctor test: a config with its timeouts removed reports out of date, is repaired to exactly what `enable` writes, then reports OK, and a second repair prints nothing.
- [x] `mise run check` (unrelated tests that time out under full-suite load each failed once and passed when rerun: `TestExternalCommand_SigintReachesPlugin`, `TestProbeConfigDir_AsksClaude`, `TestResolveClaudeConfigDir_PrefersClaudesAnswer`, and the git hook backup tests `TestInstallHooks_ForeignWrapperOverPreGuardEntireDoesNotRecurse` and `TestInstallHooks_ReclaimedChainRunsEachHookOnce`)
- [x] Manual check with the real binary in a temp repo:
  - A fresh `entire enable` reports only the installed hooks.
  - After the timeouts were removed by hand, `entire enable` and `entire doctor` each restored a file byte-for-byte identical to a fresh enable, and a second `doctor` run printed nothing.
- [x] Manual check with real Claude Code and a fake `entire` on `PATH` that hangs forever (run with an earlier 10s value for `session-start` and prompt hooks):
  - `session-start` was killed at 9.9s and `user-prompt-submit` at 10.1s.
  - `session-end` was cut off by Claude's exit limit at 1.5s, and Claude still answered.

#### not in scope

- Git hooks (`prepare-commit-msg`, `post-commit`, ...) can still hang `git commit` in this state.
- Pi already applies a flat 10s timeout in its generated extension. Whether that suits each Pi hook is better tracked in #2115.

Muskan Paliwal Wed Oct 14 11:36:23 2026 +0530
fix(claude-code): keep explicit zero hook timeouts and point hook drift to `entire agent add`

An explicit "timeout": 0 on an Entire hook read the same as no timeout, so
doctor and install replaced it and a rewrite dropped it. It is now written
back as the user wrote it.

Doctor's drift message suggested `entire enable --force`, which rebuilds
Entire's hooks and drops the timeouts and fields users set on them. A bare
`entire enable` returns early on an enabled repo, so the message now names
`entire agent add <agent>`, with --force as a fallback.

Doctor's two silent repairs share one loop, and the comment on
StatusWalkBudget is rewrapped.

Full text:

---

fixes #1065

Gives each of Entire's Claude Code hooks a timeout, so Claude Code cancels a stalled `entire` launch and keeps going instead of waiting on it. Existing installs get the timeouts from `entire doctor` or `entire agent add claude-code`, and `entire status` flags configs that still lack them and points to `entire doctor`.

#### why

In #1065, macOS blocks `entire` before Go `main()` runs (`_dyld_start`), so nothing inside the binary can time out. Without a hook `timeout`, Claude Code kept waiting on the stuck hook (still blocked after 40s in testing), and stuck hook processes piled up across sessions. With a `timeout` set, Claude Code cancels the hook and continues.

#### what changed

- Each Entire hook now carries its own timeout, from one shared table that install and repair both read. Claude Code's default is 600s for command hooks and 30s for `UserPromptSubmit`:
  - **30s** for `session-start`, which Claude blocks startup on. Besides a trail refresh capped at 1s, it resolves the repo and reads and writes session state, which a cold start or a large repo can slow well past that. This is still far below the 600s default.
  - **30s** for `user-prompt-submit`, `subagent-start` and `pre-task`, which snapshot the worktree. This matches Claude Code's own `UserPromptSubmit` default and stays above `gitrepo.StatusWalkBudget` (20s), so a slow status walk degrades on its own before the hook is cancelled.
  - **120s** for `stop`, `stop-failure`, `subagent-stop` and `post-task`, which write checkpoint data. Their path can spend up to 15s on a remote probe (`WriteProbeFetchBudget`) and 20s on a first-checkpoint status (`StatusWalkBudget`) before transcript work, and a 65MB transcript has been seen taking 30s (#2115).
  - **None** for `session-end`. Claude Code already gives exit hooks only a short time, and an explicit timeout would make it wait longer.
- New hooks are written with their timeout. A hook install (`entire agent add claude-code`, or `entire enable` when it installs hooks) adds the timeout to existing Entire hooks that have none, keeps any timeout the user set, and says it updated outdated hooks instead of "already installed".
- `entire doctor` adds the missing timeouts without asking, as it already does for the retired deny rule, and does so before its hook drift check so that check reports on the repaired config. The repair only sets a timeout on an Entire hook that has none: it adds, removes and moves no hook, keeps the user's timeouts, and skips a hook type that does not parse. It reads and writes `settings.json` through the same helpers as install, so an empty `"permissions": {}` is dropped, as install drops it.
- The Claude Code drift check used by `entire status` and `entire doctor` now reports hooks as out of date whenever a plain install would rewrite them, including Entire hooks in a command shape an older CLI wrote (which the repair does not match) and hooks without their timeout. `entire status` now suggests `entire doctor` instead of `entire enable --force` for outdated hooks, because `--force` rebuilds every Entire hook and drops the timeouts and fields the user set on them. Doctor adds missing timeouts in place, and for anything else (a missing matcher, an old command shape) it suggests `entire agent add <agent>`, with `--force` only as a fallback. It does not suggest a bare `entire enable`, which returns early on a repo that is already enabled.
- Rewriting `settings.json` keeps fields Entire does not model on the user's own hooks and matchers (for example `async`, `statusMessage`, prompt hooks). Only exact-case keys are decoded, so a key like `"Command"` is kept as written instead of overwriting `command`, and an entry whose modeled field has a value Entire does not model (a fractional `timeout`, or an explicit `"timeout": 0`) is written back unchanged. Decoding resets each entry first, so bytes kept from an earlier decode never replace the entry that followed.
- The repo's own `.claude/settings.json` is updated to match.

#### test plan

- [x] Install tests: each hook's timeout on a fresh install, timeouts added to an existing install, a user-set timeout kept, a second install not rewriting the file, user hook fields kept, and a fresh install not reported as outdated.
- [x] Field preservation: differently-cased keys and a fractional timeout survive an install unchanged, and a fractional or explicit zero timeout on an Entire hook is neither backfilled nor reported as outdated.
- [x] Repair tests: an untimed Entire hook next to a user's own matcher, a malformed hook type and a permissions block (only the timeout changes, a second run changes nothing), an empty `"permissions": {}` (dropped, as install drops it), no settings file (nothing created), and a user-set timeout (file untouched).
- [x] Drift check: missing timeouts and an older command shape both report outdated until an install fixes them.
- [x] Status hint: `entire status` points outdated hooks to `entire doctor`, not `entire enable --force` (verified RED: the output still said `run 'entire enable --force'`).
- [x] Re-decoding: decoding a clean entry into a value that held a fractional timeout writes back the clean entry (verified RED: the old `"command":"a","timeout":1.5` came back).
- [x] Doctor drift message: outdated Claude Code hooks point to `entire agent add claude-code`.
- [x] Doctor test: a config with its timeouts removed reports out of date, is repaired to exactly what `enable` writes, then reports OK, and a second repair prints nothing.
- [x] `mise run check` (unrelated tests that time out under full-suite load each failed once and passed when rerun: `TestExternalCommand_SigintReachesPlugin`, `TestProbeConfigDir_AsksClaude`, `TestResolveClaudeConfigDir_PrefersClaudesAnswer`, and the git hook backup tests `TestInstallHooks_ForeignWrapperOverPreGuardEntireDoesNotRecurse` and `TestInstallHooks_ReclaimedChainRunsEachHookOnce`)
- [x] Manual check with the real binary in a temp repo:
  - A fresh `entire enable` reports only the installed hooks.
  - After the timeouts were removed by hand, `entire enable` and `entire doctor` each restored a file byte-for-byte identical to a fresh enable, and a second `doctor` run printed nothing.
- [x] Manual check with real Claude Code and a fake `entire` on `PATH` that hangs forever (run with an earlier 10s value for `session-start` and prompt hooks):
  - `session-start` was killed at 9.9s and `user-prompt-submit` at 10.1s.
  - `session-end` was cut off by Claude's exit limit at 1.5s, and Claude still answered.

#### not in scope

- Git hooks (`prepare-commit-msg`, `post-commit`, ...) can still hang `git commit` in this state.
- Pi already applies a flat 10s timeout in its generated extension. Whether that suits each Pi hook is better tracked in #2115.

content.text:
The `entire enable` claim was wrong: a plain `entire enable` doesn't restore missing timeouts. I fixed that in the PR description, published it, then committed and pushed the test as `2a01d66a0`.

**What I tested:** I built this branch and used it in a temp repo with isolated config. After enabling Claude Code, I deleted the timeouts by hand and then ran each command:

| Command | Timeouts restored? |
| --- | --- |
| `entire enable`, with or without a terminal | No. It prints "Entire is already enabled." and doesn't touch hooks, because a bare `enable` exits early on an enabled repo (`setup.go:1435`). |
| `entire enable --agent claude-code` | Yes, identical to a fresh enable. |
| `entire agent add claude-code` | Yes, identical to a fresh enable. |
| `entire doctor` | Yes, identical, and a second run prints nothing. |

**Description changes** (two lines differ from the draft you saw):
- The install bullet now names `entire agent add claude-code` or `entire enable --agent claude-code`.
- The manual check bullet now lists those two commands and doctor as restoring the file. A new line says a bare `entire enable` leaves the file without its timeouts.

I read the description back from GitHub, and it matches what I published.

**Commit and push:**
- `2a01d66a0` has the new empty-permissions test and the rewrapped comment in `types.go`. It's pushed on top of your `51672b705`.
- Lint was clean on the final tree and the `claudecode` tests pass. I didn't re-run the full `mise run check`, because this commit only adds a test and changes comment wrapping.
- There was no trail for this PR when I checked earlier, so there were no trail findings to check after the push.
